scenes.narration: California, eighteen forty-nine. Gold! Crowds of dreamers rush into the hills with their pans. Most of them find mud. But down in town, one storekeeper is having the best year of her life. She doesn't dig. She sells the shovels. Today there's a new gold rush, and it's called AI. Everyone is watching the companies that build the chatbots. But some countries are getting rich the old way, by selling the shovels. So which countries could win the AI economy without building AI at all?

scenes.narration: That storekeeper is make-believe, but the pattern is real. In the actual Gold Rush, a merchant named Sam Brannan became known as the richest man in California. He never mined for gold. His stores sold the miners what they needed, at whatever price the rush would pay.

Meet Hattie. Her family has run the same hardware store in gold country for generations, and the old rule is still painted above the door. In a rush, sell shovels. One sleepy morning, a package lands on her counter. Inside is a tiny AI chip, the kind that runs a chatbot. And it talks. Hi, it says. I'm Nugget. I've been everywhere.

Nugget has a passport, and it's packed with stamps. Hattie flips through it. This little chip was printed on an island, with a machine from a flat green country, and memory from across the sea. Its tools and chemicals came from somewhere else again, its money from the desert, and its metal from the mountains. Every stamp is a shovel shop. Hattie grabs her hat. Let's go meet the shopkeepers.

scenes.narration: Let me draw why the shovel sellers matter. At the top, someone builds a chatbot and sells answers. To do that, they rent a data center. The data center buys chips. The chip factory buys machines, memory and chemicals. And all of it needs power, money and metal. Every dollar spent at the top rolls downhill, through the shovel shops. And here's the trick. The shops at the top have rivals everywhere. Some shops near the bottom have almost none.

First stamp, Taiwan. Nugget was born here, in a chip factory called a foundry. Its design came from America, but almost nobody else on Earth can actually build it this small. Hattie watches the line outside. The biggest names in tech, all waiting at the same counter. Excuse me, she asks. Is this the only shop? Pretty much, says Nugget.
The shop is called TSMC. Last year, it sold about a hundred and twenty billion dollars of chips, the most in its history. And every new AI model needs more of them.

The whole island feels it. Taiwan's exports smashed their record, and for the first time in twenty-six years, America became Taiwan's biggest customer, ahead of China and Hong Kong. Its biggest shipments? Servers and chips for the AI rush.
The government's statistics office now forecasts that Taiwan's economy will grow faster this year than at any time since nineteen eighty-seven. Hattie stares. All that, from selling shovels?

Being the only shop in town is powerful. It's also a little nerve-racking, for the island and for every customer in the line. We told that story in The Small Island the Whole World Economy Depends On.

Second stamp, the Netherlands. A flat, green country with one very unusual shop. Nugget's tiniest lines were printed with light, by a machine that only one company on Earth can build, ASML. Each machine is about the size of a bus, and it travels in pieces, packed into cargo planes.

scenes.narration: One of these machines costs about two hundred and fifty million dollars. And if you want the most advanced chips, there is no second shop to try. Hattie whispers. Now that's a shovel.

But even the only shop doesn't get to choose all its customers. Governments decide where these machines may go, and ASML's biggest market, China, has never been allowed the most advanced ones. We took the machine apart in The Machine Every Advanced Chip Depends On.

Third stamp, South Korea. Nugget's brain is fast, but forgetful. It needs a special memory stacked right beside it, layer on layer, like a tower of pancakes. It's called HBM. Only a handful of companies can make it, and the leader is SK hynix. I'm hungry, says Nugget. You're a chip, says Hattie.

Let me draw what the AI rush did to that one company. Not long ago, SK hynix was losing money. Memory prices had crashed. Then the rush arrived. The next year, a record. The year after that, its operating profit roughly doubled again, to about thirty-three billion dollars. For the first time, it out-earned all of Samsung.

scenes.narration: And the whole country rode along. South Korea's chip exports set a new record of about a hundred and seventy billion dollars. Hattie whistles. That's a lot of pancakes.

Fourth stamp, Japan. No famous chatbot here either. But look closer. The machines that coat, etch and clean each wafer, from companies like Tokyo Electron. The ultra-pure chemicals and the light-sensitive coatings that chip factories everywhere depend on. Japanese companies make most of them.

Japan's shovel shops rarely make headlines. They make the parts nobody can skip. Quiet, steady, and very hard to copy. We opened that cabinet in The Chemicals Nobody Talks About That Decide Who Makes Chips, and Japan's robot bet in Will AI Make Japan Rich Again?

Fifth stamp, the Gulf. Here the shovel isn't a machine. It's money, and sunshine. Funds built on oil money are now pouring it into AI. Hattie peeks inside a vault. It's not gold, says Nugget. It's better. It's patient.
An Abu Dhabi investment company called MGX is one of the founding backers of Stargate, a plan announced to spend up to five hundred billion dollars on AI data centers in America.

And at home, the region is building giant AI campuses in the desert, powered by cheap sunshine and gas. Saudi Arabia's sovereign fund launched an AI company of its own, called HUMAIN. The bet is simple. If you can't make the shovels, own a piece of every shop. We followed the power side in Could Cheap Electricity Become the New Oil?

Sixth stamp, the mountains of Chile. Giant trucks haul copper ore up out of the pit. Copper is the wire inside every data center, every power line and every chip package. And Chile mines almost one in every four tons of copper on Earth.
Across the ocean, Australia digs up about a third of the world's lithium, the metal in the batteries that back up power grids, phones and electric cars.

Here's the twist. The International Energy Agency forecasts that the copper mines already planned could fall about a third short of demand by the middle of the next decade. A shortage sounds like a jackpot for Chile.

scenes.narration: But a mine can't charge whatever it likes. Copper is sold at one world price. When the rush runs hot, every mine wins. When it cools, the price falls for everyone at once. Nugget gulps. So metal is a shovel anyone can sell.
Back to the Gold Rush. What happened to Sam Brannan? Years later, his empire collapsed, and he died poor. The shovel seller had ridden the rush all the way up, and all the way down.

It happens with chips too. Remember SK hynix losing money? That was a memory crash, when buyers paused and prices fell off a cliff. We told that story in The Three Companies That Decide How Much Your Memory Costs.

So which shovels last? Let me draw it. On one side, the shovels anyone can sell. Metal, money, power. Their price rises and falls with the rush. On the other side, the shovels nobody else can make. The foundry, the machine, the most advanced memory. Those shops get to set their own price. The safest shovel isn't the biggest one. It's the one with no second shop.

scenes.narration: Hattie writes up her scorecard. Taiwan and the Netherlands, winning, as long as nobody builds a second shop and politics stays calm. South Korea, winning big, on a rollercoaster. Japan, steady and hard to replace. The Gulf, buying a seat at every table. Chile and Australia, rich in the good years, exposed in the bad ones.

So can a country win the AI economy without building AI? Yes. Some already are. But the winners aren't the ones who dig the most. They're the ones who own a shovel nobody can copy, and keep inventing the next one before the rush moves on.
Back home, Hattie repaints the sign above her door. Nugget hops onto the counter. So what do we sell now? Hattie smiles. Whatever they can't get anywhere else.
